title: Case 1: Governors of States (7th Amendment Dual-State Office) (Article 153 • Writ Petition)
factualMatrix: Before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32), an aggrieved petitioner challenged an impugned executive notification and enforcement order issued by the Union Ministry / Central Authority under Article 153 (Governors of States (7th Amendment Dual-State Office)) of Part VI (The States). Relying on the core guarantee that Mandates a Governor for each State, enabling one person to be appointed Governor for two or more States under the 7th Constitutional Amendment, 1956. and citing B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010), the petitioner sought judicial invalidation for violating constitutional limits and procedural fairness.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Writ Petition before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32) is maintainable under Article 153?
2. Does the Union Ministry / Central Authority's executive notification and enforcement order conform to Article 153 (Governors of States (7th Amendment Dual-State Office))?
3. How does B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) govern the constitutional validity and relief in this matter?
statutoryApplicability: B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY: The Writ Petition before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32) is maintainable as it raises a direct constitutional question under Article 153 (Part VI).

2. SUBSTANTIVE ANALYSIS (Article 153): Mandates a Governor for each State, enabling one person to be appointed Governor for two or more States under the 7th Constitutional Amendment, 1956. Applying the governing principle—'Dual constitutional role of the Governor: Nominal head of the state executive and agent of the Union government.'—the impugned executive notification and enforcement order by the Union Ministry / Central Authority must strictly satisfy constitutional bounds.

3. PRECEDENT (B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010)) & RELIEF: Guided by B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010), any overreach inconsistent with Article 153 is liable to be quashed or suitably restrained.

markingRubric.criterion: Precedent reasoning (B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010)) & relief
